question: Why would a nurse choose to give a medication by injection instead of getting the patient to swallow pills?

options.A: Lower risk of local tissue damage
options.C: Elimination of the need for sterile equipment
options.D: Extended duration of drug action in the gut

explanation: Great job! Injections skip the digestive system entirely, meaning the drug gets right into the blood and starts working much faster. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h1)

question: As a nursing student, you know that keeping things strictly aseptic during injections is vital. Why?

options.A: It speeds up the chemical reaction of the drug in the body
options.B: It prevents the needle from becoming blunt during insertion
options.C: It prevents introducing pathogens directly into sterile body tissues
options.D: It ensures the medication dissolves completely in the syringe

explanation: Spot on! Because a needle goes right past the skin barrier, any germs on the skin or equipment can easily cause deep, painful infections if we aren't sterile. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h1)

question: When giving an intramuscular (IM) injection to an adult, which site is usually the safest and most recommended?
explanation: You've got this! The ventrogluteal site is clear of major nerves and large blood vessels, making it the safest spot for deep muscle injections. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h2)

question: You are about to give a routine vaccine to a chubby 12-month-old infant. Which IM injection site is best?
explanation: Correct! The vastus lateralis (thigh muscle) is well-developed in babies and is the safest, go-to spot for infant IM injections. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h2)

question: What angle should you hold your needle when giving a standard intradermal injection (like a Mantoux test)?
explanation: Nice one! Intradermal shots need a very shallow angle so the medication sits right under the top layer of skin, forming a little bleb. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h3)

question: Why is the subcutaneous tissue layer great for medications like insulin?

options.A: It reacts violently with all types of water-soluble medications
options.B: It has sparse blood supply, causing slower and sustained absorption
options.C: It lacks nerve endings, preventing any sensation of fluid entry
options.D: It contains dense muscle fibers that rapidly push drugs into veins

explanation: Spot on! Because fat tissue doesn't have a massive blood supply, it releases medications slowly and steadily over time, which is just what insulin needs. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h3)

question: Looking at different needle sizes, which gauge is the thinnest?
explanation: You nailed it! Remember: the higher the gauge number, the thinner the needle. A 27-gauge needle is very fine compared to a thick 16-gauge needle. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h4)

question: Why do modern syringes come with safety-engineered devices?

options.A: To prevent the medication from leaking out of the syringe barrel
options.B: To make the needle sharper for easier penetration through thick skin
options.C: To reduce the risk of accidental needle-stick injuries to healthcare workers
options.D: To guarantee that the exact volume of medication is injected into the patient

explanation: Exactly! These built-in shields and guards protect us nurses from accidental pricks after we finish giving an injection. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h4)

question: What special equipment do you need when drawing up medication from a glass ampoule?
explanation: Correct! Snapping open a glass ampoule creates tiny invisible glass shards. A filter needle catches them so they never reach your patient. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h5)

question: Before you pull medication out of a multi-dose vial, why do you inject air into it first?

options.A: To sterilize the rubber stopper before the needle enters
options.B: To activate the chemical properties of the powdered drug
options.C: To dilute the concentration of the medication inside the vial
options.D: To create positive pressure that makes fluid withdrawal easier

explanation: You've got this! Pumping air in replaces the volume of liquid you're taking out, stopping a vacuum from forming so the medicine flows smoothly. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h5)

question: What is the main reason a nurse uses the Z-track technique for an intramuscular injection?

options.A: To speed up the absorption rate of water-soluble drugs
options.B: To seal the medication within the muscle and prevent leakage
options.C: To eliminate the need to cleanse the skin with an antiseptic
options.D: To reduce pain by numbing the nerve endings in the skin

explanation: Spot on! The Z-track method locks irritating medications deep inside the muscle so they don't leak back up into sensitive skin tissues. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h6)

question: Right before you insert the needle in a Z-track injection, what do you do with your non-dominant hand?

options.A: Massaging the injection site vigorously with an alcohol swab
options.B: Warming the medication vial in the palm of the hand
options.C: Pulling the skin and subcutaneous tissue laterally
options.D: Pinching a large fold of skin between thumb and finger

explanation: Great job! Pulling the skin to the side before poking creates a zig-zag path that traps the medication inside the muscle afterward. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h6)

question: Which of these is considered a very unsafe practice when handling used needles on the ward?

options.A: Carrying a single-handed scoop method for recapping
options.B: Recapping used needles using both hands
options.C: Activating safety shields immediately after administration
options.D: Disposing of uncapped needles into a rigid sharps box

explanation: Correct! Using two hands to recap a used needle is a major hazard—it's one of the easiest ways to accidentally stab yourself. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h7)

question: You just finished giving an IM injection to a patient. What should you do immediately with the used syringe and needle?

options.A: Place the syringe on the bedside table for later disposal
options.B: Detach the needle by hand and throw it in the regular trash
options.C: Drop the entire unit immediately into a nearby sharps container
options.D: Recap the needle tightly and store it in the pocket for safety

explanation: You nailed it! Always drop the whole syringe and needle straight into the sharps box without removing or bending anything. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h7)

question: When charting an injection in a patient's nursing notes, which detail is NOT necessary to write down?

options.A: The exact time the medication was given
options.B: The patient's immediate response to the drug
options.C: The brand name of the syringe used
options.D: The specific anatomical site of the injection

explanation: Spot on! We need to record the drug, dose, time, site, and how the patient felt, but the brand of the syringe doesn't matter for their medical record. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h8)

question: Why is it important to spend a few minutes monitoring your patient right after giving an injection?

options.A: To check if the skin surface has cooled down to normal body temperature
options.B: To detect early signs of severe allergic reactions or adverse effects
options.C: To ensure the patient does not walk around the ward too quickly
options.D: To evaluate whether the patient enjoyed the interaction with staff

explanation: Brilliant! Because injected drugs get into the body fast, we need to stay close in case a sudden allergy or bad reaction pops up. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h8)
